bib.title: Brain-Inspired Graph Multi-Agent Systems for LLM Reasoning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Brain-Inspired Graph Multi-Agent Systems for LLM Reasoning" (BIGMAS), Guangfu Hao, Yuming Dai, Xianzhe Qin, Shan Yu (CASIA/UCAS), arXiv:2603.15371v1 [cs.AI], 16 Mar 2026. Preprint (the header carries no venue; the format looks like IEEE).
COVERAGE: 55,156 of 55,156 chars read (the text before ~47,500 in full, then the references skimmed for origins). It has about 10 pages and no appendices; the paper has no ablation section or appendix tables. Fig 3 values were read from the extracted bar labels.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Wrapping a model in BIGMAS raised accuracy for all six models on all three tasks, with no exceptions.
  number: DeepSeek-V3.2 25->36 (Game24), 12->30 (Six Fives), 6->20 (ToL). Claude 4.5 Sonnet 48->68, 15->38, 40->46. GPT-5 96->100, 95->100, 91->98. Claude 4.5 (+thinking) on ToL 57->93.
  setup: 100 instances per benchmark, single run each as far as stated, so there are no seeds and no confidence intervals on accuracy. Models: DeepSeek-V3.2 (with and without thinking), Claude 4.5 Sonnet (with and without thinking), Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5. Temperature 0.7 for all BIGMAS calls. The base condition is one direct call.
  quote: "BIGMAS consistently improves performance across all models and tasks without exception." and "Claude 4.5 (+thinking) shows the most dramatic improvement on Tower of London, rising from 57.0% to 93.0%"
  where: Sec IV.A, p5-6, Fig 3
- Against multi-agent baselines, BIGMAS wins by modest margins. The DeepSeek-V3.2 numbers are in Table I.
  number: Base 25/12/6, ReAct 26/18/10, ToT 30/25/18, BIGMAS 36/30/20 (Game24 / Six Fives / ToL)
  setup: DeepSeek-V3.2 only, 100 instances per task. ReAct: max 10 turns, temperature 0.7. ToT: max_rounds=4, n_thoughts=3, temperature 0.7. No token or compute matching is reported between methods.
  quote: "BIGMAS surpasses Tree of Thoughts by 6.0%, 5.0%, and 2.0% on Game 24, Six Fives, and Tower of London, respectively"
  where: Sec IV.B, Table I, p6
- The GraphDesigner builds task-specific topologies whose size tracks task difficulty.
  number: nodes per graph, mean±SD: Game24 3.07±0.38, Six Fives 3.87±1.12 (range 3-9), ToL 4.82±1.47 (range 2-9)
  setup: all instances and all six models pooled. The designer is capped at MAX_NODES=10 and MAX_PATH_LENGTH=15.
  quote: "Game 24 graphs cluster tightly around three nodes (mean 3.07±0.38)... Tower of London exhibits the broadest distribution (two to nine nodes, mean 4.82±1.47)"
  where: Sec IV.C, Fig 4, p6
  Note: the text also says "without any explicit complexity constraints", yet Sec III.E sets the node and path caps. These two statements sit in tension.
- The designed graph shapes differ by task. Game24 gets a generate-validate-format pipeline. The largest Game24 example (6 nodes) has parallel brute-force and heuristic branches feeding one shared validator. ToL gets a 9-node cyclic graph (BFS-style move enumeration, candidate selection, move validation). Six Fives gets a 9-node multi-stage refinement chain.
  quote: "from compact three-node generate–validate–format pipelines for Game 24 to nine-node cyclic structures for Tower of London"
  where: Sec IV.C and V, Fig 5
- Node roles shift with the task.
  number: Generator 34% / Validator 32% / Formatter 31% on Game24. On ToL, Analyzer 24%, Optimizer 12%, Formatter at least 19% on every task.
  setup: share of all nodes across all designed graphs.
  quote: "Tower of London exhibits the most diverse role composition: Analyzer nodes rise to 24% and Optimizer nodes to 12%"
  where: Sec IV.D, Fig 6
- Coordination has a token cost. Execution takes about half of the tokens, orchestrator routing takes a bounded share, and graph design is a fixed up-front cost.
  number: node execution 46.4% / 50.9% / 55.5% of tokens (Game24 / Six Fives / ToL). Routing 16.9%-25.2%. Graph design 36.7% (Game24) vs 18.9% (ToL).
  setup: pooled over six models. Absolute tokens per run reach about 22k (Game24), 200k (Six Fives) and 600k (ToL) at the high end of the axes in Fig 7.
  quote: "Node Execution dominates total token expenditure across all tasks, accounting for 46.4%, 50.9%, and 55.5%"
  where: Sec IV.E, Fig 7
- Failing runs make more orchestrator routing calls than passing runs. This could serve as an early-stopping signal, but the paper does not test it.
  number: failed vs correct mean routing decisions: Game24 1.2 vs 1.6 (as printed), Six Fives 1.9 vs 4.5, ToL 7.3 vs 9.4. Mean routing per run: 1.3 / 2.6 / 7.9, with a ToL maximum of 49.
  setup: pooled over models. Fig 9 shows Incorrect needing more routing calls than Correct.
  quote: "The gap between failed and successful runs is modest for Game 24 (1.2 vs. 1.6 decisions on average), pronounced for Six Fives (1.9 vs. 4.5), and substantial for Tower of London (7.3 vs. 9.4)."
  where: Sec IV.F, p7
  Warning: the sentence assigns the lower number to failed runs in the Game24 and Six Fives pairs and the higher number to failed runs in the ToL pair. That contradicts the text on either side, which says incorrect runs need more routing. The order of the numbers is probably reversed (correct first) in the text, or the text is wrong. Do not cite the direction with confidence. Check Fig 9 against the PDF, or use the qualitative claim only.
- Design (architecture mechanics, no numbers).
  - The Workspace is one shared object with four partitions: B_ctx (read-only problem context), B_work (read-write), B_sys (step count and routing history), B_ans (sink-only).
  - Agents never talk point to point.
  - Each node emits a structured write instruction (path, action, payload). The action is append, update or replace.
  - A validator checks the path exists, the action fits the field type, and the payload is non-empty. On failure the node is re-invoked with the error, up to R times. A failed write never changes the workspace.
  - Routing is deterministic when a node has one successor. With more than one successor, an LLM Orchestrator reads the full workspace plus the execution history.
  - A step budget Tmax is enforced, and a FallbackResolver picks the best candidate if the budget runs out.
  - The GraphDesigner also writes a natural-language "workspace contract" κ that states each node's read and write duties. Graphs may contain cycles.
  quote: "All agent nodes interact exclusively with B; no point-to-point communication between nodes occurs." and "The Workspace state is never modified by a failed write, preserving integrity throughout execution."
  where: Sec III.B-D, Algorithm 1, p3-5

LIMITS
- The authors concede: only three combinatorial puzzle benchmarks. They list open-domain QA, competition maths and code as future work. The GraphDesigner has no memory across instances. Tmax and R are fixed. Total token cost exceeds single-model inference ("total token cost exceeds single-model inference").
- Not shown: any ablation separating the contributions of dynamic graph design, the shared workspace, and the global orchestrator. The "synergy" claim is asserted, not isolated. No comparison with a fixed-topology graph that uses the same workspace. No cost-matched comparison with ToT or self-consistency. The baselines were run on DeepSeek-V3.2 only. No variance, seeds or significance tests, on 100 instances per task. Absolute token cost per run is shown only in box plots. The claim of "orthogonal" gains rests on this evidence alone. Tool-using or open-ended tasks are not tested.
- Inconsistencies: Table I's DeepSeek row (25/36, 12/30, 6/20) matches Fig 3. The "without any explicit complexity constraints" wording conflicts with the node and path caps. The routing numbers above are internally ambiguous.
- "Four of six models reach 100% on Game24": this is read from the Fig 3 labels (DeepSeek+think, Gemini, GPT-5 and Claude+think are shown at 100).
- Dated: models are late-2025 (Claude 4.5, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2). The paper calls itself "the first to operationalize all three" GWT properties, a novelty claim that is unverified.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Global Workspace Theory: Baars 1988 (A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness, Cambridge Univ. Press); Dehaene and Changeux 2011 (Neuron 70).
- Tree of Thoughts, Yao et al., NeurIPS 2023. This is also the source of Game24.
- ReAct [25]; Reflexion [26]; Graph of Thoughts, Besta et al. [28]; Buffer of Thoughts [29]. Check these entries for venues and years in the reference list.
- MetaGPT, Hong et al., ICLR 2024 (printed as "twelfth ICLR, 2023").
- GPTSwarm, Zhuge et al., ICML 2024 (agents as optimizable graphs).
- DyLAN [35]; LLMCompiler [30]; AutoGen [32]; CAMEL [33]; multiagent debate [34]; Plan-and-Act, Erdogan et al. 2025 [52].
- Shojaee et al. 2025, "The Illusion of Thinking", arXiv 2506.06941. This is the motivating source for accuracy collapse.
- Tower of London task: [46].
- Chain-of-Thought: Wei et al., NeurIPS 2022.

CODE: No code released. Only pseudocode: Algorithm 1 "BIGMAS Execution" (p5), with the loop: node execute -> Validate -> up to R self-correct retries -> Apply to B -> Orchestrator routing; if the step budget is exhausted, FallbackResolver. The write instruction is ω=(π,α,δ), with α in {append, update, replace}. The paper's Fig 2 labels δ = ast.literal_eval.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p4) "Overview of the BIGMAS framework": shows graph design (GraphDesigner), the four-partition workspace, and execution (validate, self-correct, route). The best single figure for the target note: it shows the blackboard, the task-specific graph, and the orchestrator in one picture.
- Fig 5 (p7) shows example designed topologies for each task (Game24 6 nodes, Six Fives 9, ToL 9). It is the best illustration of task-specific topology, if the note wants one.

PROBLEMS: pypdf printed a harmless fontTools warning. Figure axes and labels extract as scattered text. No embedded instructions found. Fig 9's exact bar values cannot be read from the extraction, so the failed-versus-correct routing direction needs checking against the figure.
